readerTitle: Why watching a struggling employee more closely can make things worse
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Manzoni & Barsoux, 1998 '실패하도록 설계된 증후군') + 가상 사례 (B2B 마케팅 에이전시, 배관 서비스 회사). 실제 기업의 정확한 사례를 확보하기 어려워 company_story 대신 '선의의 대응이 역효과를 낸다'는 반례 형식을 택함.
insight: 성과 부진은 판결할 대상이기 전에 진단할 신호다. 기대가 분명했는지, 할 수 있는 조건이 있었는지를 먼저 확인하면 대응이 달라진다.
misconception: 일을 못하는 직원은 더 가까이 감시하고 통제하면 나아진다. 또는 문제가 커질 때까지 기다렸다가 평가 때 말하면 된다.

sources.text: Manzoni, J.-F., & Barsoux, J.-L. (1998). The Set-Up-to-Fail Syndrome. Harvard Business Review, March–April 1998.
에이전시와 배관 서비스 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Manzoni & Barsoux(1998)의 핵심 주장(상사가 특정 직원을 약하다고 판단하면 더 가까이 감독하고, 직원은 이를 신뢰 부족으로 읽어 위축되며, 그 결과가 상사의 판단을 확인해 주는 악순환)을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 연구의 비율이나 수치를 일부러 넣지 않았습니다.

가상 사례의 이름(Dana, Marco)과 상황은 모두 설명용입니다. 수치는 사용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why watching a struggling employee more closely can make things worse
body: Dana, an account manager at a small marketing agency, missed three client deadlines in a month. Her boss did what felt responsible: he started checking every email and report before it went out.
Two months later, Dana was slower, quieter and missing more deadlines than before.

image.label: A manager looking over an employee's shoulder as her desk piles up
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실 책상에 앉은 직원 뒤에서 상사가 어깨 너머로 화면을 들여다봄. 직원 책상 위 서류 더미가 점점 높아지고 직원은 몸을 움츠림. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your account manager keeps missing deadlines.
body: Dana was solid for two years. Lately, client reports arrive late and one client has complained.
What do you do first?

options.text: Review all her work before it goes to clients
options.feedback: This protects clients this week. But it adds a delay, and it tells Dana you've lost confidence before you know what's wrong.

options.text: Meet privately, name the specific gap, ask what's getting in the way, and agree on a check-in date
options.feedback: You act early and stay specific, and you learn the cause before choosing a fix. It costs an awkward conversation now instead of a bigger one later.

options.text: Give it time and raise it at her review next quarter
options.feedback: You avoid friction today. Meanwhile the gap grows, teammates cover for her, and the review lands as a surprise.

cards.title: The fix fed the problem.
body: Once every report needed approval, Dana stopped making calls on her own. She waited for sign-off, and sign-off took days. She stopped suggesting ideas in meetings.
Her boss read this as proof she couldn't cope, so he checked even more closely.
Nobody had asked the first question. Dana had been handed two new clients with no change to her old workload. The real problem was capacity, not skill.

cards.title: Handling underperformance
body: **Handling underperformance** well starts by treating a gap as a question, not a verdict. Before you pick a fix, check three things:
list: **Clarity:** does the person know what good looks like, by when?
**Capability:** do they have the skill, tools and time to do it?
**Circumstance:** is something else in the way, such as workload, a personal issue or lost motivation?
cards.callout: Each cause needs a different fix. Closer supervision fixes none of them.

cards.title: The set-up-to-fail loop
body: In a 1998 Harvard Business Review article, researchers Jean-François Manzoni and Jean-Louis Barsoux described a pattern they called the **set-up-to-fail syndrome**.

Once a boss decides someone is weak, the boss supervises more and gives less freedom. The employee reads this as distrust, pulls back and takes fewer risks. Their work slips, which confirms the boss's view.
The boss usually means well. That's what makes the loop hard to see from the inside.

image.label: A loop: boss doubts, controls more, employee withdraws, work slips
image.brief: 원형 순환 다이어그램. 네 칸: "Boss doubts" → "More control" → "Employee pulls back" → "Work slips" → 다시 "Boss doubts". 화살표가 점점 진해져 악순환을 표현. 단순한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Early, specific, and written down.
body: Talk while the gap is small. Describe what happened, not who the person is: "three reports were late," not "you're unreliable."
Then agree on what good looks like, what support you'll give and when you'll check in together. Write it down so both of you remember it the same way.
Either outcome is useful. Performance improves, or you both see clearly that the role isn't working.
cards.softwareNote: A "slow" engineer may be working from vague tickets or carrying a heavy on-call load. Look at the specs and the interruptions before you judge the person.

cards.title: Diagnosis is not endless patience.
body: Asking about causes can turn into an excuse to never decide. Set a timeframe. If expectations were clear, support was real and nothing changed, a move to another role or an exit is fairer than months of drift.
Teammates notice when a gap goes unaddressed, and they often absorb the extra work.
For formal warnings or exits, follow your company's process and local rules.

cards.title: Now it's a plumbing company.
body: Marco, one of your technicians, gets far more callbacks than the rest of the team. Customers phone back because the leak wasn't fixed.
What's your best first move?

options.text: Send him on a general plumbing refresher course
options.feedback: Training helps if the cause is skill. If he's rushing because his route is overbooked, you've spent money and fixed nothing.

options.text: Walk through his last few callback jobs with him, find the pattern, then agree on a target and support
options.feedback: You find the actual cause first, whether that's skill, parts or time per job. It takes an hour of your time, but the fix will fit the problem.

options.text: Quietly give him only simple jobs without saying why
options.feedback: Callbacks may drop for now. But Marco never learns what's wrong, others take the hard jobs, and the gap stays hidden.

cards.softwareNote: The same move works for a support agent whose tickets keep reopening: review a few reopened tickets together before choosing a fix.

cards.title: Diagnose before you decide.
body: When someone falls short, check clarity, capability and circumstance first. Then act early, be specific and set a date to review.
**Try it today:** think of one person whose work worries you. Write one sentence on what good looks like, and ask yourself whether they've ever heard it from you.
